theme_intro: This week is about trust and meaning. Believers get depressed too: Elijah, David, Jeremiah and Job all cried out, and the research shows that faith is often a real help in depression, though never a shield against it. Each day offers one honest, small step that works whether or not you believe, alongside any treatment you are receiving.

days.title: Believers get depressed too
days.quote: Believing in God, accepting Jesus' gift of salvation, and being filled with the Spirit do not necessarily spare us from mental pain and suffering.
days.quote_source: Bergland & Jónsson, Adventist Review, “Why Do We Get Depressed?”
days.explanation:
After the greatest day of his life, the prophet Elijah walked into the desert, lay down under a bush and asked God to let him die (1 Kings 19:4). David wrote, “My tears have been my food day and night.” Jeremiah cursed the day he was born. Jesus, in Gethsemane, said his soul was sorrowful “even unto death.” The Bible does not hide these moments. It keeps them.

Two Adventist psychiatrists put it plainly in the Adventist Review: believing in God does not necessarily spare us from mental pain. Depression is an illness of brain, body and life circumstances, and it visits believers as readily as anyone else. Having it says nothing about the quality of your faith.

What does the research say? The largest review, by Bonelli and colleagues, covered 444 studies from 1962 to 2011. About six in ten found that people with a more active faith had less depression or recovered faster; about one in three found no clear link; six in a hundred found more depression. So faith is often a resource, and it is not a vaccine. A UK review of the same literature calls the benefit real but “often modest.”

Notice what God did for Elijah. No sermon. Sleep, then food, then a touch, then a second meal, then a quiet voice. If you are thinking about ending your life today, please call a crisis line; the Help page has your country's number.
days.challenge: Read 1 Kings 19:1-8 slowly, on your phone or in a Bible, and notice what God did for Elijah before saying a word about his calling: sleep, bread, water, a touch, more sleep. Then do one Elijah thing for yourself today: eat something simple, drink a glass of water, or lie down for 20 minutes without guilt. If that is too much today, read only verses 5 to 7 and let “the journey is too great for thee” be your permission to rest.
reflection_questions: When you read that Elijah asked to die and God answered with sleep and food, what do you feel?
Who first told you, in words or in silence, that depression means weak faith? Do you still believe them?
What is one “Elijah thing” your body has been asking for?

scripture.text: And the angel of the LORD came again the second time, and touched him, and said, Arise and eat; because the journey is too great for thee.

days.title: When faith hurts and when it heals
days.quote: In some populations or individuals, however, religious beliefs may increase guilt and lead to discouragement as people fail to live up to the high standards of their religious tradition.
days.explanation:
Underneath the headline that faith helps, the research has a quieter finding. Faith can hold you, and faith can be turned into a stick to beat yourself with. Which one it is matters more than how often you attend.

Bonelli's team found that in some groups, especially people struggling with family trouble, religious involvement went with more depression, probably because it stirred up guilt. A UK review of the literature reached the same conclusion from the other side: the forms of spirituality that help are those that promote hope, forgiveness and purpose; those that produce guilt, shame or powerlessness can harm, and a guilt- or punishment-based picture of God goes with more anxiety.

The research also separates two kinds of faith. Intrinsic faith is the inner trust that gives life meaning; extrinsic faith is the outward sign, such as being seen at church. In the studies summarised by Peselow and colleagues, only intrinsic faith predicted a shorter time to remission. Trust, not performance.

So when a voice inside says “God is punishing you” or “a real Christian would not feel this,” hear it for what it is: depression speaking with a religious accent. Scripture's own picture is different. Elijah was fed, not rebuked. Isaiah describes a God who will not break a bruised reed or snuff out a smoking wick. Jesus called the exhausted to come to him. Trust and struggle can live in the same heart. Struggle is not failure.
days.challenge: Take a piece of paper or the journal in this app. On the left, write one sentence your depression says about God or about you, for example “God is disappointed in me.” On the right, write what you would say to a close friend who said that sentence about herself. Read the right-hand side aloud once. Then read Isaiah 42:3. If that is too much today, read the verse twice and leave the paper for another day.
reflection_questions: Which picture of God did you grow up with, and does it look like the one in Isaiah 42:3?
When has your faith carried you, and when has it felt like a weight?
What would change if you treated struggle as part of faith rather than its opposite?

scripture.text: A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench: he shall bring forth judgment unto truth.

days.title: Lament: giving words to pain
days.quote: My tears have been my food day and night, while they continually ask me, “Where is your God?”
days.explanation:
Many of the Psalms, perhaps a third, are laments: prayers that start in the dark and stay there for a while. Psalm 88 never reaches a happy ending; its last words are “my friends into darkness.” Psalm 13 opens with “How long?” Job asked why he had not died at birth. Jeremiah asked why he ever left the womb. On the cross, Jesus prayed a lament, Psalm 22: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” None of this was edited out. It is Scripture.

That matters in depression, because depression takes your words. You feel a weight and cannot name it; you feel far from God and assume the distance is your fault. A lament lends you words until your own return. In Swinton's interviews with depressed Christians, people described how familiar prayers and liturgy “carry a person through” their worst moments when their own mind could not supply faith. One woman said: “God became a friend… everything, I discussed with God… it's how I survived.”

Honest complaint is a form of trust. You do not shout at someone you believe is absent. Bergland and Jónsson write of a God who “is present and suffers with the sufferer.” Paul adds that when we do not know how to pray, the Spirit prays for us with groanings that cannot be put into words (Romans 8:26).

If you do not believe, the practice still works. Pain written down is pain held somewhere outside your head.
days.challenge: Write your own lament today, in four short lines, in the journal or on paper. Line one: who you are speaking to (“God,” or “to whoever is listening”). Line two: what hurts, in plain words. Line three: what you need. Line four: one thing you remember being true, even if you cannot feel it now. Ten minutes at most; spelling and theology do not matter. If that is too much today, copy out Psalm 13:1 in your own handwriting and stop there.
reflection_questions: Which line of your lament was hardest to write, and why?
Were you taught that complaining to God is unfaithful? Where did that teaching come from?
What does it mean to you that Psalm 88 was kept in the Bible without its ending being fixed?

scripture.text: Yahweh is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit.

days.title: Faith and medicine together
days.quote: Belief in God, but not religious affiliation, was associated with better treatment outcomes.
days.explanation:
Some believers quietly fear that seeing a doctor or a therapist means their faith has failed. The evidence points the other way: faith and treatment work together, and faith often helps treatment work better.

Rosmarin and colleagues followed 159 patients in a psychiatric day programme at a Harvard teaching hospital. Those who believed in God were more likely to respond to treatment, and their depression and self-harm fell further. The reason was telling: believers trusted the treatment more and expected it to help, and that expectation carried much of the benefit. Belonging to a denomination on paper predicted nothing; belief did.

Peselow's team watched 84 depressed outpatients through eight weeks of antidepressant treatment. Believers improved by about 57 percent on the main depression scale, non-believers by about 34 percent, and the more spiritual a patient was, the more their hopelessness lifted. The authors are honest that the study was small, that believers started out less ill, and that it cannot prove cause.

Anderson's review pooled 16 randomised trials of faith-adapted CBT, where the therapist uses the patient's own scriptures and prayer inside standard cognitive therapy. It beat waiting lists, and for religious patients it did somewhat better than ordinary CBT in several trials. But the trials were small and mostly run by the people who designed the therapy, so the reviewers urge caution. In every trial comparing the two, both groups ended in the non-depressed range. Good therapy helped either way.

Luke, who wrote a Gospel, was a physician. Asking for help is a form of trust.
days.challenge: If you are already seeing a doctor or therapist, write one sentence today about what your faith means to you in this illness, and bring it to your next appointment. You may ask whether your faith can be part of the work. If you are not yet getting help, find the phone number of your GP or a counsellor and write it on the first page of your journal. If that is too much today, say aloud once: “Getting help is not a lack of faith.”
reflection_questions: What have you believed about faith and medicine, and where did you learn it?
What would you want a doctor or therapist to understand about your faith?
Who in your life could walk with you to a first appointment, or sit with you afterwards?

scripture.text: He heals the broken in heart, and binds up their wounds.

days.title: A small purpose for today
days.quote: Suffering ceases to be suffering at the moment it finds a meaning.
days.quote_source: Viktor Frankl, Man's Search for Meaning (quoted in Peselow et al., 2014)
days.explanation:
Depression drains meaning. Bergland and Jónsson describe it exactly: “What provides meaning and enjoyment in life fades.” Things you used to care about turn grey, and the question “what is the point?” hangs over everything.

Viktor Frankl, who survived four concentration camps, taught that people can bear almost anything if they can find a why. Peselow's team, reflecting on their study of depressed patients, concluded that spirituality works partly as “a system of meaning” which insists that circumstances are not senseless. In a large review, 42 of 45 studies found a link between faith and a sense of meaning and purpose.

Martin Seligman's positive psychotherapy goes further and suggests that lack of meaning is not only a symptom of depression but one of its causes. His definition is useful: meaning comes from using your strengths to belong to and serve something bigger than yourself, whether God, family, church or community. In a small pilot study, depressed clients who received this therapy reached remission more often than those in usual care, though the numbers were tiny and need repeating.

The Overcoming Depression workbook suggests writing a personal mission statement: your values and priorities in a sentence or two, not written in stone. In depression, shrink it. Not a mission for life, a purpose for today. “Today I am someone who keeps one promise.” “Today I am someone who prays for one person by name.” Zechariah asks who has despised the day of small things. God has not.
days.challenge: Write one sentence that begins “Today I am someone who…” and finish it with something small and true to your values: who keeps one promise, who is kind to one person, who prays for one neighbour by name. Then do one 10-minute act that fits it: send the message, water the plant, make the call. If that is too much today, write only the sentence and put it where you will see it tomorrow morning.
reflection_questions: What gave your days meaning before depression? Is any piece of it still within reach?
Who or what do you belong to that is bigger than you?
What is the smallest act today that would still count?

scripture.text: For who hath despised the day of small things?

days.title: Forgiveness and rest
days.quote: Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.
days.explanation:
Depression carries two heavy loads most people never mention to their doctor: old resentments, replayed at three in the morning, and a tiredness so deep that no one gives you permission to rest from it. Faith has something to say about both.

Forgiveness first. Bonelli's review notes that religious involvement goes with greater forgiveness and gratitude, and forgiveness therapy is among the spiritual interventions tested for depression. Seligman's positive psychotherapy includes a forgiveness exercise, because a grudge keeps a painful memory alive and replaying. The UK literature review found that the forms of spirituality that help are those that promote “hope, forgiveness and purpose.”

Be clear about what forgiveness is not. It is not pretending the hurt did not happen, and it is not going back to someone unsafe. It is deciding to stop collecting a debt you were never going to be paid, a decision you may need to make more than once. Depression also runs up a debt against yourself; that one needs releasing too.

Then rest. God rested on the seventh day, and Jesus said the Sabbath was made for people, not people for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27). Rest is not laziness; it was God's first medicine for Elijah. In Mills' study of 186 heart patients, spiritual wellbeing went with better sleep and lower depression, and the link ran largely through gratitude. If you have energy for neither prayer nor Bible reading, rest in God's presence without words. That counts.
days.challenge: Choose one of two acts today. Either write the name of someone you resent, perhaps your own, and under it the sentence “I release you from this debt today”; keep the paper, do not send it. Or plan 20 minutes of real rest: no screen, no task, lying down or sitting by a window, treated as something prescribed. If that is too much today, rest for five minutes with your hand on your chest and breathe slowly.
reflection_questions: What debt have you been trying to collect, and what has it cost you to carry it?
When did you last rest without feeling guilty? What made that possible?
What would a Sabbath hour look like for you this week?

scripture.text: He said to them, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.”

days.title: Weeping for a night, held by others
days.quote: Weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning.
days.explanation:
Depression lies about time. Bergland and Jónsson name it as a common symptom: the conviction that this will never end. Abraham Lincoln, in its grip, wrote “I am now the most miserable man living.” He went on to lead a nation. Nights in depression are long, but they are still nights.

The research adds something practical about how people reach morning: rarely alone. Cruwys and colleagues followed more than 5,000 older adults in England. Depressed people who belonged to no group and joined one cut their risk of relapse by about a quarter; joining three cut it by about two thirds. A congregation is exactly such a group, and more. The UK literature review describes the support of a faith community as something that can accompany a person “from birth to death.” One interviewee said: “Church is like a family… we'll get through this together.” In Bonelli's review, 61 of 74 studies linked faith with stronger social support.

When Moses' arms grew too heavy, Aaron and Hur held them up (Exodus 17:12). Bergland and Jónsson say the depressed may need others to hold up hope for them. That is not weakness; it is how the body of Christ is meant to work.

Next week is about getting help: doctors, therapy, medication. A WHO manual tells group leaders to give hope without false promises; that is our aim too. If you are thinking about ending your life, please call a crisis line today; the Help page has your country's number.
days.challenge: Make one small commitment today: send one message to one person in your faith community, or a trusted friend, saying something like “I have been struggling lately. Could we talk this week?” You may add “Would you pray for me?” if that fits you. Note in your journal who you wrote to and when. If that is too much today, write the person's name and the day you will send it, and tell God, or the page, that you mean it.
reflection_questions: Who has held up your arms before, even briefly?
What stops you from letting someone in your community know how you really are?
Looking back on this week, which day's idea do you want to carry into next week?

scripture.text: Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.
